set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What are the four Centor criteria?
opts: Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and ABSENCE of cough
Correct. Three are things present and one is a thing absent, which is the part most often misremembered.
Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and PRESENCE of cough
Cough counts when it is ABSENT — a cough points away from streptococcal infection and toward a viral cause.
Fever, sore throat, headache and myalgia
Sore throat, headache and myalgia are not the criteria; Centor scores fever, exudates, anterior cervical nodes and no cough.
Fever, trismus, uvular deviation and drooling
Those suggest a peritonsillar abscess rather than the scoring rule for pharyngitis.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Amber fluid behind the tympanic membrane, sometimes with visible bubbles. What is this finding?
opts: Blood behind the membrane from temporal bone fracture
Blood behind the membrane looks dark rather than amber, and it follows trauma rather than an upper respiratory infection.
Cerumen visible through a perforation
Wax sits in the canal, in front of the membrane rather than behind it.
Serous effusion
Correct. A serous effusion is amber fluid behind the eardrum, sometimes with bubbles, brought on by an upper respiratory infection or a change in atmospheric pressure.
Purulent effusion from acute otitis media
A purulent effusion goes with a red, bulging membrane that has lost its landmarks.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A patient reports ear pain but the ear itself looks entirely normal. Which structures should the history now cover?
opts: The jaw joint, the teeth and the cervical spine
Correct. Ear pain is frequently referred, and these three are the usual sources — the first answer a patient gives is not the last question you ask.
The frontal and maxillary sinuses
Sinus tenderness is part of the nose examination. Referred otalgia comes from the joint, the teeth and the cervical spine.
The thyroid gland and the trachea
Both belong to the neck examination; referred ear pain comes from the jaw joint, the teeth and the cervical spine.
The parotid and submandibular salivary glands
The salivary glands are not among the referred sources. The cranial nerves that carry the referral are V, VII, IX and X.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which epistaxis history suggests a SYSTEMIC problem rather than a local one?
opts: Bleeding from one nostril after digital trauma
Bleeding after digital trauma is a local cause; recurrence, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere, suggests a systemic problem.
Bleeding that follows a recent upper respiratory infection
Inflammation after an infection is a local cause of epistaxis, like trauma, dry mucosa, a foreign body or a tumor.
Bleeding in dry winter air
Dry mucosa is a local cause; a systemic problem is suggested by recurrent bleeding or bleeding and bruising elsewhere.
Recurrent bleeding, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere on the body
Correct. One nosebleed is local until proven otherwise; a pattern of bleeding at other sites changes the question entirely.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A smooth, beefy red tongue points to which deficiency?
opts: Vitamin D
Vitamin D deficiency is not the cause; a smooth, beefy red tongue is the sign of vitamin B12 deficiency.
Vitamin B12
Correct. The appearance is atrophic glossitis, and it earns a look for the rest of the deficiency picture.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency affects the gums rather than the tongue surface; the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to B12.
Iron alone
Iron deficiency has its own oral signs, but the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to vitamin B12.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How does the course of CENTRAL vertigo differ in duration from the peripheral causes?
opts: Variable, but rarely continuous
Correct. Central vertigo runs a variable course but is rarely continuous, whereas each peripheral cause has a characteristic duration.
Always continuous until treated
Central vertigo is variable but RARELY continuous, so a course that is always continuous does not fit it.
Always under one minute
Episodes under one minute are the benign positional vertigo pattern; central vertigo is variable in duration.
Always several hours
Episodes of several hours to a day or more fit Ménière disease; central vertigo is variable and rarely continuous.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How is the auricle positioned to straighten the ear canal for otoscopy in an adult?
opts: Pull it down and back
That is the maneuver for an infant, whose canal runs differently.
Press it forward against the cheek
Pressing the auricle forward does not straighten the canal; the auricle is pulled up, back and away from the head.
Leave it undisturbed and advance the speculum slowly
Without straightening the canal the speculum meets the canal wall, which is both painful and uninformative.
Pull it up, back, and away from the head
Correct — all three directions. The canal is not straight, and the view is only as good as the alignment.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What is microtia?
opts: An extra accessory auricle
An extra accessory auricle is a supernumerary auricle, a separate congenital deformity; microtia is an abnormally small auricle.
A small pit anterior to the tragus
A small pit in front of the ear is a preauricular sinus or pit; microtia is an abnormally small auricle.
An abnormally small auricle
Correct. Microtia is a congenitally underdeveloped, abnormally small auricle, and it is grouped with atresia among the congenital deformities.
An absent or closed ear canal
That is atresia, which often accompanies microtia but is a separate finding.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How is the RINNE test performed, in order?
opts: Fork on the vertex of the head, then moved to the mastoid
The top of the head is where the Weber fork goes; Rinne starts on the mastoid and then moves close to the canal.
Fork held in front of both ears simultaneously
Rinne tests one ear at a time and compares two positions on that ear.
Fork on the mastoid until the sound stops, then beside the canal
Correct. Bone conduction comes first, with the fork on the mastoid until the sound stops; the fork then moves close to the canal and the patient is asked if it is still heard.
Fork close to the canal first, then on the mastoid once the sound stops
The sequence starts at the mastoid, testing bone conduction first.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which statement about discharge in acute sinusitis is correct?
opts: Green discharge is diagnostic of bacterial infection
Discharge color is not diagnostic, so green discharge does not prove bacterial infection; purulence is only suggestive.
Clear discharge excludes sinusitis
Clear discharge does not exclude sinusitis, because discharge color is not diagnostic in either direction.
Discharge is absent in acute sinusitis
Nasal discharge is one of the suggestive features of acute sinusitis, along with local tenderness, pain and fever.
Purulent discharge is suggestive
Correct, and the distinction matters — patients and clinicians both over-read green discharge as proof of bacterial infection. But the COLOR of the discharge is not diagnostic.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What does “disequilibrium” mean, as distinct from vertigo and presyncope?
opts: Anxiety-driven dizziness
That is the psychiatric category, which also covers depression and substance use.
Unsteadiness or imbalance
Correct. Disequilibrium is unsteadiness or imbalance, without the spinning of vertigo or the faint, lightheaded feeling of presyncope.
A spinning sensation
A spinning sensation is vertigo; disequilibrium is unsteadiness or imbalance without any sense of rotation.
Feeling faint or lightheaded
Feeling faint or lightheaded is presyncope; disequilibrium is unsteadiness or imbalance without faintness.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: FINE hair and COARSE hair on examination point to which conditions?
opts: Fine hair to hypothyroidism; coarse hair to hyperthyroidism
Reversed: fine hair points to hyperthyroidism and coarse hair to hypothyroidism.
Both to hypothyroidism
The two textures point in opposite directions: fine hair to hyperthyroidism, coarse hair to hypothyroidism.
Both to nutritional deficiency
Hair texture here reflects thyroid status: fine hair suggests hyperthyroidism, coarse hair hypothyroidism.
Fine hair to hyperthyroidism; coarse hair to hypothyroidism
Correct — a small finding, but it is examined for at the same moment as the scalp and the skull.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: An abnormally ENLARGED head raises which two conditions?
opts: Hydrocephalus and Paget disease
Correct. One expands the skull from within, the other thickens the bone itself.
Microcephaly and hydrocephalus
Microcephaly is an abnormally small head; an enlarged head raises hydrocephalus and Paget disease.
Hypothyroidism and acromegaly
Hypothyroidism and acromegaly are not causes of an enlarged head; those are hydrocephalus and Paget disease.
Paget disease and microcephaly
Microcephaly belongs with a small head, not an enlarged one, which raises hydrocephalus and Paget disease.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Why should recent dental work be asked about when a patient presents with facial pain?
opts: Dental infection is the commonest cause of frontal sinusitis
The link is with the maxillary sinuses, not the frontal ones; recent dental work may affect the maxillary sinuses.
Dental work may affect the maxillary sinuses
Correct. The maxillary sinus floor sits directly above the upper tooth roots, so a dental procedure can present as sinus pain.
Dental anesthetic commonly causes anosmia
Anosmia is asked about separately in the nose history; it is not tied to dental anesthetic.
Dental work is a recognized cause of epistaxis
Dental work is not an epistaxis cause; those are trauma, inflammation, dry mucosa, foreign body and tumor.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Where is the fork placed for the WEBER test?
opts: Just outside the ear canal, to test air conduction alone
Air conduction alone is the second half of Rinne, not Weber.
Behind the ear on the occiput, to test both ears simultaneously
The occiput is not used; for Weber the base of the fork sits on the top of the head or the mid-forehead.
On the top of the head or mid-forehead
Correct. The base of the fork sits on the top of the head or mid-forehead, and the test evaluates unilateral hearing loss by lateralization.
On the mastoid process, to compare bone against air conduction
A fork on the mastoid comparing bone with air conduction is the Rinne test; Weber uses the top of the head or mid-forehead.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How is transillumination of the MAXILLARY sinus performed?
opts: In a dark room, shine the light down below the inner eye corner
Correct. In a dark room the light shines down just below the inner corner of the eye, with the patient's mouth open.
In a dark room, shine the light up under the brow close to the nose
Shining the light up under the brow close to the nose is the frontal sinus technique, not the maxillary one.
In a bright room, shine the light through the cheek from the side
A dark room is required, and the light is placed below the medial canthus.
Shine the light into the nostril and look at the forehead
Shining the light into the nostril tests nothing; the maxillary sinus is lit from below the medial canthus.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which description of exostoses is correct?
opts: Cholesterol deposits in the middle ear
Exostoses are not middle-ear deposits of any kind. They are benign bony growths, and they sit in the canal.
Benign bony growths in the ear canal, causing conductive loss
Correct. They narrow the canal mechanically, which is why the loss is conductive.
Benign bony growths on the ossicles, causing sensorineural loss
They are canal growths, and any canal problem produces conductive loss.
Malignant bone tumors of the temporal bone
Exostoses are benign bony growths in the canal; a malignant temporal bone tumor is a different problem entirely.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A firm raised lesion at an old ear piercing site. Which description fits?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma — more common in darker-skinned individuals
Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy, and the association runs the other way.
A keloid — scar tissue, more common in darker-skinned individuals
Correct. Keloids are commonest on the shoulders and upper chest but arise at piercing sites, which puts them on the ear.
Tophi — and there is no skin-type association
Tophi are uric acid deposits of chronic tophaceous gout, not related to piercing.
A cutaneous cyst — more common in darker-skinned individuals
Cutaneous cysts are usually epidermoid or pilar and carry no such association.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Nasal polyps are associated with which conditions?
opts: Asthma, aspirin sensitivity and cystic fibrosis
Correct. Nasal polyps are associated with allergic rhinitis, aspirin sensitivity, asthma, chronic sinus infection and cystic fibrosis.
Hypertension, anticoagulation and atherosclerosis
Hypertension, anticoagulation and atherosclerosis are not polyp associations; polyps go with asthma, allergy and cystic fibrosis.
Smoking, alcohol and reflux
Smoking, alcohol and reflux relate to hoarseness and tobacco history; polyps go with asthma and aspirin sensitivity.
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnea
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnea are not polyp associations; polyps go with allergy, aspirin sensitivity, asthma and cystic fibrosis.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Under what symptom duration is acute BACTERIAL sinusitis unlikely?
opts: Less than four weeks
Four weeks is the boundary between acute and subacute disease, not the bacterial threshold.
Less than twelve weeks
Twelve weeks is not the threshold; acute bacterial sinusitis is unlikely when symptoms have lasted under seven days.
Less than seven days
Correct. Most cases under a week are viral, which is the single most useful piece of timing in the nose section.
Less than three days
Three days is too short a threshold; acute bacterial sinusitis is unlikely whenever symptoms have lasted under seven days.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What accompanies the vertigo of Ménière disease, beyond the vertigo itself?
opts: Dysarthria and ataxia
Dysarthria and ataxia are brainstem deficits that go with central vertigo; Ménière disease is a peripheral cause.
Pressure or fullness in the affected ear
Correct. Ménière disease brings pressure or fullness in the affected ear, with fluctuating tinnitus and a sensorineural loss that recurs and eventually progresses.
Nystagmus alone, with normal hearing
Nystagmus occurs but hearing is not normal — it recurs and eventually progresses.
Impaired hearing on one side with cranial nerve V and VII involvement
One-sided hearing loss with cranial nerve V and VII involvement is the acoustic neuroma picture, not Ménière disease.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What is a NORMAL Rinne result?
opts: Bone conduction heard longer than air conduction
Bone conduction outlasting air conduction is the conductive hearing loss result, not the normal one.
Both heard for exactly the same duration
Equal duration is grouped with the conductive finding, not the normal one.
Neither heard, in a quiet room
A normal patient hears both, and hears the tone longer through air than through bone.
Air conduction heard longer than bone conduction
Correct. Normally sound is heard longer through air than through bone, so air conduction outlasts bone conduction.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: At what age do conductive and sensorineural hearing loss typically begin?
opts: Both typically begin in childhood
Only conductive loss begins in childhood and young adulthood; sensorineural loss usually begins in middle or later years.
Conductive up to about forty; sensorineural in later years
Correct. Conductive loss usually begins in childhood and young adulthood, up to age 40, and sensorineural loss in middle or later years.
Conductive in middle or later years; sensorineural in childhood
Reversed. Sensorineural loss is the later-onset pattern, and conductive loss is the one that shows up from childhood to about forty.
Both typically begin after sixty
Only sensorineural loss typically begins in middle or later years; conductive loss begins in childhood, up to about age 40.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which viral infections cause SENSORINEURAL hearing loss?
opts: Rubella and cytomegalovirus
Correct — both damage the inner ear, and both matter most when the exposure was congenital.
Rhinovirus and influenza
These cause upper respiratory infection, which contributes to serous effusion — a conductive problem.
Respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus
Respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus are not the viral causes of sensorineural loss; those are rubella and cytomegalovirus.
Herpes simplex and varicella zoster
Herpes simplex and varicella zoster are not the viral causes of sensorineural loss; those are rubella and cytomegalovirus.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which part of the examiner's hand should rest against the patient during otoscopy?
opts: The palm, to steady the patient's head
The anchoring is of the instrument against the head, and it is the ulnar border of the hand that makes the contact.
The thumb, to hold the auricle in position
The other hand holds the auricle. The ulnar aspect of the otoscope hand makes the contact.
No part — the otoscope is held clear of the patient
Holding it clear is exactly what makes a sudden movement dangerous.
The ulnar aspect
Correct. The ulnar aspect of the hand contacts the patient, anchoring the otoscope so a sudden movement does not drive it into the canal.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Vertigo comes on when the patient rolls onto one side in bed, lasts under a minute, and hearing is unaffected. Which is it?
opts: Benign positional vertigo
Correct. Sudden onset on rolling onto the affected side or tilting the head up, a few seconds to under a minute, hearing not affected, tinnitus absent.
Ménière disease
Ménière runs several hours to a day or more, and hearing IS affected.
Vestibular neuronitis
Vestibular neuronitis begins suddenly but runs from hours to up to two weeks, not seconds to under a minute.
Acoustic neuroma
Insidious, with impaired hearing on one side and tinnitus present.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A MULTINODULAR enlarged thyroid carries a risk of malignancy under what circumstance?
opts: Only if the gland is tender
Tenderness points to thyroiditis; a multinodular gland raises malignancy risk when there is a family history.
Only in patients under thirty
Age is not the qualifier; a multinodular enlarged thyroid raises malignancy risk when there is a family history.
When there is a family history
Correct — the multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process, and family history is what raises the concern.
Always, regardless of history
A multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process; it is a family history that raises the concern about malignancy.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which three findings together describe the tympanic membrane in acute otitis media?
opts: Pale, thickened and immobile
Thickening describes chronic change; the acute picture is redness and bulging.
Amber with visible bubbles
That is a serous effusion, without the redness of acute infection.
Red, bulging, and with the landmarks lost
Correct. The purulent effusion behind it pushes it outward and obscures the normal anatomy.
Red, retracted, and with the landmarks exaggerated
Retraction with exaggerated landmarks is the opposite picture — negative middle ear pressure pulling the membrane inward.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A chalky white patch on the tympanic membrane of a patient who once had tympanostomy tubes. Which interpretation is correct?
opts: Tympanosclerosis — and it always requires referral
The patch is tympanosclerosis, but it is usually not clinically significant, so it does not always require referral.
A cholesteatoma — and it requires urgent referral
A cholesteatoma is a keratin mass behind or through the membrane, not a flat chalky patch, and it does not follow tube placement.
A healing perforation — which will close spontaneously
The deposit follows severe otitis media or a healed perforation; it is not itself an open perforation.
Tympanosclerosis — usually not significant
Correct. Tympanosclerosis is a hyaline deposit in the membrane after severe otitis media or a healed perforation, and it is usually not clinically significant.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Submandibular swelling and erythema with cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. Which description fits?
opts: A submandibular stone — the danger is infection
A stone causes obstruction and swelling at meals, not spreading cellulitis.
Ludwig's angina — it is life threatening because of the AIRWAY
Correct. The swelling pushes the tongue and floor of mouth upward and back, and the airway is the reason this cannot wait.
Ludwig's angina — the danger is spread to the mediastinum only
Ludwig's angina is right, but its life-threatening danger is the airway, not spread to the mediastinum.
A peritonsillar abscess — the danger is rupture
A peritonsillar abscess deviates one tonsil; it is not a floor-of-mouth cellulitis.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A patient's own voice is UNUSUALLY LOUD. Which kind of hearing loss does that suggest?
opts: Neither — loud voice indicates a psychiatric cause
A loud voice is a feature of sensorineural loss, where hearing is difficult; it does not indicate a psychiatric cause.
Sensorineural
Correct. In sensorineural loss the voice may be loud because hearing is difficult, including hearing one's own voice.
Conductive — the middle ear amplifies the patient's own voice
In conductive loss the voice stays SOFT, because the inner ear and cochlear nerve are intact and bone conduction carries the patient's own voice perfectly well.
Either — voice volume does not distinguish them
It does distinguish them, and it costs nothing to notice while taking the history.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What does GENERALIZED lymphadenopathy raise?
opts: Otitis media and otitis externa
Otitis media and otitis externa drain to specific node groups, producing regional rather than generalized enlargement.
Thyroiditis and goiter
Thyroiditis and goiter are thyroid findings; generalized lymphadenopathy raises causes such as lymphoma and leukemia.
Human immunodeficiency virus
Correct. Generalized lymphadenopathy raises human immunodeficiency virus infection, Epstein-Barr virus, lymphoma, leukemia and sarcoidosis.
Dental infection and tonsillitis
Dental infection and tonsillitis cause regional node enlargement; generalized enlargement raises lymphoma or leukemia.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Why should dentures be removed during the oral examination?
opts: To assess the fit of the denture itself
Denture fit is not the reason; dentures come out so the mucosa beneath them can be checked for ulcers and lesions.
To allow the tongue blade to be inserted
The tongue blade is for seeing the posterior pharynx; the dentures come out so the mucosa beneath them can be inspected.
To let the patient speak more clearly during the history
Speech is not the reason; dentures are removed so the mucosa beneath them can be inspected for ulcers and lesions.
To look underneath for ulcers and lesions
Correct. A denture hides exactly the mucosa most at risk from chronic irritation.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which causes produce CENTRAL vertigo?
opts: Otitis media, otitis externa and Eustachian tube dysfunction
Middle and external ear disease — these cause ear pain, not central vertigo.
Brainstem lesion, atherosclerosis and multiple sclerosis
Correct — all vascular, demyelinating or structural problems above the inner ear, with vertebrobasilar migraine and transient ischemic attack completing the list.
Benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease and labyrinthitis
Benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease and labyrinthitis are all peripheral causes arising in the inner ear.
Loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, salicylates and alcohol
Loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, salicylates and alcohol cause drug toxicity vertigo, which is a peripheral cause.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A patient says others mumble, and that they struggle most in a noisy restaurant. Which kind of hearing loss does that pattern suggest?
opts: Sensorineural
Correct. Sensorineural loss brings trouble understanding speech, complaints that others mumble, and hearing that worsens in noisy environments.
Conductive — noise masks the residual hearing
The opposite. In conductive loss a noisy environment may actually HELP, because the background is attenuated along with everything else.
Mixed loss, which always presents this way
No pattern is specific to mixed loss; the history described points to the sensorineural component.
Neither — this is a description of tinnitus
Tinnitus is sound with no external source. This patient is describing difficulty with external sound.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which features mark vertigo as CENTRAL rather than peripheral?
opts: Hearing impaired on one side with tinnitus present
That combination points peripheral — acoustic neuroma in particular.
Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position
Brief episodes set off by rolling over or tilting the head describe benign positional vertigo, a peripheral cause.
Aural fullness with fluctuating tinnitus
Ear fullness with fluctuating tinnitus is Ménière disease, a peripheral cause in which hearing is also affected.
Brainstem deficits such as dysarthria and ataxia
Correct. Central vertigo usually comes with other brainstem deficits (dysarthria, ataxia, crossed motor and sensory deficits), while hearing is unaffected and tinnitus absent.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Why does a septal hematoma require URGENT drainage?
opts: To prevent secondary sinusitis
Infection is not the reason for urgency; drainage is urgent to prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage.
To prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage
Correct. The cartilage has no blood supply of its own — it depends on the lining that the hematoma has stripped away, so the clock starts immediately.
To prevent the blood tracking into the orbit
Orbital spread is not the reason; drainage is urgent to prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage.
To prevent airway obstruction
Obstruction may occur but is not why the drainage is urgent.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which cranial nerves carry referred pain to the ear?
opts: III, IV and VI
The ocular motor nerves. They have no sensory supply to the ear.
VIII alone
Cranial nerve VIII is vestibulocochlear — hearing and balance, not pain sensation.
XI and XII
Accessory and hypoglossal — motor nerves to the shoulder and tongue.
V, VII, IX and X
Correct. Four nerves supply sensation to the ear, which is exactly why disease well away from the ear can present as otalgia.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What does the canal look like in ACUTE otitis externa?
opts: Swollen, narrow, moist, pale and tender, and it may be erythematous
Correct. The swelling and tenderness dominate, and the narrowing is often what makes the examination difficult.
Thickened, red and itchy
That is the CHRONIC picture. The acute canal is swollen and painful rather than thickened and itchy.
Dry, scaly and pale, with no tenderness
Tenderness defines acute otitis externa, in which the canal is swollen, narrow, moist and pale rather than dry.
Normal, with the abnormality confined to the tympanic membrane
Otitis externa is a disease of the canal, which is precisely how it is distinguished from middle ear disease.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: How do you confirm the otoscope has no leaks BEFORE inserting it for insufflation?
opts: Compare the bulb pressure against the other otoscope
Comparing instruments does not test this otoscope; place a finger over its speculum tip and squeeze the bulb instead.
Place a finger over the speculum tip and squeeze the bulb
Correct. If the bulb squeezes freely with the tip blocked, air is escaping somewhere and the test will be uninterpretable. Resistance means no leak.
Squeeze the bulb in open air and listen for a hiss
Air moves freely in open air whether or not the system leaks, so this shows nothing.
Insert the speculum and watch the membrane; no movement means a leak
That confuses a leaking instrument with a genuinely immobile membrane — which is the finding you are trying to detect.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: How does a septal hematoma form?
opts: Chronic inflammation erodes the septum until it bleeds
Erosion through the septum describes a perforation, caused by trauma, surgery or drug use, not a hematoma.
Venous engorgement of the turbinates spreads to the septum
Turbinate engorgement is not the mechanism; a hematoma is blood collecting between the septal lining and the cartilage.
Injured vessels bleed between the lining and the cartilage
Correct. Injury disrupts the blood vessels and pulls the lining away from the cartilage, allowing blood to collect between the two.
Blood collects within the cartilage itself
Blood does not collect inside the cartilage; it collects between the septal lining and the cartilage beneath it.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which three structures are inspected and palpated before the otoscope is picked up?
opts: The parotid gland, the temporomandibular joint and the zygomatic arch
The temporomandibular joint matters for referred pain on history; the ear exam inspects and palpates the auricles, mastoid and tragus.
The preauricular, postauricular and occipital nodes
Those nodes belong to the neck lymph node examination; the ear itself is inspected and palpated at the auricle, mastoid and tragus.
The auricles, the mastoid and the tragus
Correct. Tenderness found here localizes disease before anything is put into the canal, and tragal tenderness in particular points to the canal itself.
The tympanic membrane, the ossicles and the cochlea
None of these can be inspected or palpated from outside; the first is seen only through the otoscope.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What result on the whispered voice test counts as normal?
opts: Normal is six of six correct; anything less is abnormal
Six of six is not required; three or more correct out of six already counts as a normal whispered voice test.
Normal is one of six correct
One of six correct would be a markedly abnormal result; the normal threshold is three or more.
Normal is any response at all; the test is qualitative
The test is scored, not qualitative: three or more of six correct is normal and four of six incorrect is abnormal.
Normal is three or more of six correct
Correct. Normal is three or more of six correct, and four of six incorrect is abnormal; the three-item sequence is whispered twice.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which pairing of usual cause and accompanying finding fits a tympanic membrane perforation?
opts: Cerumen impaction, with pain through the perforation
Cerumen blocks the canal and does not perforate the membrane; perforation usually follows otitis media, with drainage.
Otitis media, and drainage may come through the perforation
Correct. The perforation is usually the consequence of middle ear disease rather than a primary event.
Otitis externa, with itching through the perforation
Otitis externa is confined to the canal and does not perforate the membrane.
Barotrauma, with vertigo through the perforation
Atmospheric pressure change brings on serous effusion; perforation usually follows otitis media, with drainage through it.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: How long does benign positional vertigo last overall, as opposed to how long a single episode lasts?
opts: Episodes last hours, and the condition lasts a few weeks
Episodes lasting several hours or more fit Ménière disease; a benign positional vertigo episode is under a minute.
Episodes and the condition both last a few weeks
The defining feature of positional vertigo is precisely how BRIEF each episode is.
Each episode is under a minute, but the condition lasts a few weeks and may recur
Correct. Each episode comes on over a few seconds to under a minute, but the condition itself lasts a few weeks and may recur.
Each episode is under a minute, and the condition resolves within 24 hours
Too short. Benign positional vertigo lasts a few weeks rather than a day, and it may recur after settling.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A raised, shiny, slow-growing lesion on the auricle with visible telangiectasia. What should be suspected?
opts: A tophus
A tophus is a hard uric acid nodule of chronic tophaceous gout, not a shiny lesion with telangiectasia.
Basal cell carcinoma
Correct. Raised, shiny, telangiectatic and slow growing — and malignant, which is what separates it from the benign lumps in the same list.
A cutaneous cyst
A cutaneous cyst is benign, usually epidermoid or pilar; raised, shiny and telangiectatic points to basal cell carcinoma.
A keloid
Scar tissue, typically at a site of previous injury or piercing.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: The Weber test is done and the patient hears the tone only in the LEFT ear. Which ear has sensorineural hearing loss?
opts: Neither — this is a normal result
A normal result is midline or heard in both ears; hearing the tone in one ear only means it has lateralized.
Both
Weber evaluates unilateral loss; a bilateral symmetrical loss would not lateralize.
The right
Correct. Sensorineural loss lateralizes AWAY from the damaged side, so hearing the tone on the left places the lesion on the right.
The left
That would be true for a conductive loss, which lateralizes TOWARD the affected side.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A patient speaks unusually SOFTLY despite a hearing complaint. Which loss does that point to?
opts: Presbycusis specifically
Presbycusis is sensorineural, and would make the voice loud.
Conductive — the inner ear and cochlear nerve are intact
Correct. In conductive loss the voice remains soft because the inner ear and cochlear nerve are intact, so the patient's own voice is heard normally.
Sensorineural — the patient compensates by speaking quietly
The opposite: sensorineural loss tends to make the voice loud, because hearing is difficult for the patient.
Mixed loss only
A soft voice is a feature of conductive loss, where the inner ear and cochlear nerve are intact; it is not specific to mixed loss.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which statement correctly sorts migraine, tension and cluster headaches by their EPISODIC and UNILATERAL patterns?
opts: Migraine and cluster are episodic; migraine and tension are unilateral
The pairings are swapped: migraine and tension are episodic, while migraine and cluster are unilateral.
All three are episodic and all three unilateral
Not all three share both features: migraine and tension are episodic, and migraine and cluster are unilateral.
Only cluster is episodic and only tension unilateral
Cluster is not the only episodic one, and tension is episodic, not unilateral; migraine and cluster are unilateral.
Migraine and tension are episodic; migraine and cluster are unilateral
Correct. Migraine appears in both lists, which is why the two features have to be taken together rather than either alone.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What kind of pressure is applied to the bulb during pneumatic otoscopy?
opts: As hard as the patient will tolerate
Force is not what makes the membrane move visibly, and it hurts.
A series of rapid repeated squeezes
Repeated squeezing is not the technique; apply quick, firm but gentle pressure to the bulb and watch the membrane move.
Quick, firm but gentle
Correct. Only a small pressure change is needed; the membrane's movement is slight, and force adds nothing but discomfort.
Slow and sustained, held for several seconds
A sustained squeeze equalizes rather than producing the brief deflection you are watching for.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which description fits a typical tongue cancer?
opts: On the lateral border or undersurface, as an indurated lesion
Correct. Tongue cancers are usually indurated red or white lesions on the lateral border or undersurface, typically in males over 50.
On the dorsum, as smooth red patches, in females under thirty
The dorsum and smooth red patches are wrong; cancers sit on the lateral border or undersurface, usually in males over 50.
At the tip, as painful ulcers, in any age group
Painful ulcers at the tip are more typical of aphthous ulceration.
On the undersurface, as blue tortuous swellings
Blue tortuous swellings under the tongue are varicose veins; cancer appears as an indurated red or white lesion.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which causes of hoarseness should a history cover?
opts: Viral laryngitis, overuse, reflux, nerve damage, smoking
Correct — a list that runs from the trivial to the serious, which is why hoarseness always earns a full history.
Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis and chronic postnasal drip
Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis and postnasal drip are nasal conditions, not the causes of hoarseness a history covers.
Gingivitis and dental caries
Gingivitis and caries are gum and tooth findings; hoarseness comes from laryngitis, overuse, reflux, nerve damage or smoking.
Presbycusis and tinnitus
Presbycusis and tinnitus are hearing symptoms; hoarseness is a voice symptom with causes such as laryngitis and reflux.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Why does the ABSENCE of cough count toward the Centor score rather than its presence?
opts: A cough indicates the infection has spread to the lower airway
The criterion is about separating bacterial from viral pharyngitis, not about tracking spread to the lower airway.
Cough is a criterion only in children
Absence of cough scores for any patient; age enters the modified score separately, not through cough.
A cough points toward a viral cause
Correct. A cough points toward a viral cause, so its absence raises the probability of streptococcal pharyngitis and scores a point.
Coughing masks tonsillar exudates on examination
Cough does not hide exudates, which score as their own criterion; the rule separates streptococcal from viral sore throat.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is known by which other names?
opts: Ludwig's angina, and quinsy
Ludwig's angina is a floor-of-mouth cellulitis; quinsy is a peritonsillar abscess.
Angular cheilitis, and perleche
Angular cheilitis is cracking at the corners of the mouth; this gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth.
Aphthous stomatitis, and canker sores
Canker sores are aphthous ulcers; necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth.
Vincent's angina, and trench mouth
Correct. Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth, a painful, severe gum infection with rapid tissue death.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What causes a PERFORATED nasal septum?
opts: Trauma, surgery or drug use
Correct. All three destroy the septal blood supply or the cartilage itself, and drug use is the one patients do not volunteer.
Allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis
Allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis inflame the mucosa without destroying the cartilage underneath it.
A foreign body lodged for several days
A foreign body causes unilateral obstruction rather than perforation; septal perforation comes from trauma, surgery or drug use.
Repeated epistaxis from Kiesselbach's plexus
Bleeding from the anterior septum does not itself perforate it.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A patient says they are “dizzy”. Which four categories must the history separate?
opts: Vertigo, migraine, seizure and syncope
Migraine and seizure are not dizziness categories; the four are vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and psychiatric causes.
Peripheral vertigo, central vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss
This splits vertigo into its own subtypes but omits the non-vestibular causes, which is the whole reason for asking.
Orthostatic, cardiac, neurological and metabolic
A reasonable clinical list, but it splits by mechanism rather than by what the patient is actually describing.
Vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and psychiatric causes
Correct. The word means nothing until the patient explains it, and these are the four things it turns out to mean.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A tympanic membrane perforation that does NOT extend to the margin is called what?
opts: Central
Correct. The classification is simply by whether the margin is involved, and a marginal perforation is the one that does involve it.
Marginal
Marginal perforations are the ones that DO involve the margin.
Attic
Attic is not one of the two positions; perforations are central if they spare the margin and marginal if they involve it.
Traumatic
Trauma describes a cause, not a position; perforations are classed as central or marginal by whether they reach the margin.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A diffusely enlarged, FIRM thyroid points to what?
opts: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Correct. Firmness is the feature that separates it from Graves, where the gland is soft.
Graves disease
Graves disease gives a soft diffuse enlargement; a firm, diffusely enlarged gland points to Hashimoto thyroiditis.
A multinodular goiter
A multinodular goiter is nodular rather than diffuse; firm diffuse enlargement points to Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Thyroid carcinoma
A single hard nodule would raise that, not diffuse firm enlargement.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What frequency pattern does presbycusis take?
opts: Higher frequency loss
Correct, and it is why the complaint is about clarity rather than volume — the high registers carry the consonants.
Lower frequency loss
Presbycusis takes the higher frequencies, not the lower ones, so the higher registers are lost and sound may be distorted.
All frequencies equally
The loss is not flat across frequencies; presbycusis is a higher frequency loss, so sound may be distorted.
Loss confined to the speech range, sparing higher and lower tones
Presbycusis is a higher frequency loss, not a loss confined to the middle of the speech range.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What is the Rinne result in CONDUCTIVE hearing loss?
opts: Bone conduction is heard but air conduction is heard longer
Air conduction lasting longer is the normal ratio, which also holds in sensorineural loss; conductive loss gives bone equal to or longer than air.
Bone conduction equal to or greater than air conduction
Correct. Bone conduction equals or outlasts air conduction, because vibrations through bone bypass the impaired external or middle ear to reach the cochlea.
Air conduction greater than bone conduction
That is the normal pattern, which also persists in sensorineural loss.
Neither is heard at all
Conductive loss reduces air conduction; it does not abolish hearing by bone.
